text: The system observes recent workload behavior and selects an existing scheduling policy. It keeps the policy implementations separate from the learning layer.

AutoScheduler studies whether a compact model can observe recent workload behavior and choose among existing CPU scheduling policies. The current result is a validated research prototype, not a deployed kernel scheduler.
One fixed policy cannot serve every workload equally well
Policy prediction and scheduler tuning can improve workload-specific outcomes [1], [4].
Learned routers can choose among expert policies while stability filters limit rapid switching [2].
Recent systems separate learned control from a small execution path [3], [6].
A lightweight selector, observed-only features, guarded switching, and one shared simulator for all policy comparisons.
Prior work: [1] Biswas et al.  [2] Wang et al.  [3] Fu et al.  [4] Lee et al.  [6] Seo et al.

Static schedulers make different trade-offs. AutoScheduler builds on policy prediction, learned routing, adaptive priority control, parameter tuning, and interpretable safety controls.

Model comparison: scheduling outcome decides the prototype
Accuracy means agreement with the deterministic lowest-cost action. Raw accuracy did not choose the winner.
Decision Tree produced the lowest validation scheduling score: 0.120669.
Captured traces: Ridge and Decision Tree tied on cost and action agreement. Decision Tree had lower P99 latency, while the configured simplicity rule selected Ridge.

The controlled grouped split shows that action accuracy and scheduling outcome can disagree. Decision Tree has the lowest validation scheduling score, so the prototype freezes it. In the separate captured-trace bake-off, Ridge and Decision Tree tie on realized cost and action agreement. The configured simplicity rule selects Ridge, even though the tree has lower measured P99 inference time.

Classifier tree and policy-cost tree answer different questions
Directly proposes one scheduler from the observed state.
Predicts every scheduler's cost, then selects the minimum estimate.
Classifier tree, because its validation scheduling score and response time were better. The policy-cost tree remains an evaluated alternative.

The classifier optimizes direct policy choice. The policy-cost tree estimates each candidate action. The classifier is frozen for the demonstration because it produced the lower validation scheduling score and much lower P95 response, even though the policy-cost tree had lower test action regret and fewer starvation events.

alt: Dynamic V3 CPU execution timeline for the unseen changing workload

text:
This demonstration uses an unseen changing workload with CPU-intensive, interactive, and batch phases. The router reviews the observed state every 10 ticks. Confidence, a 20-tick minimum dwell, and safe dispatch boundaries limit switching. The result proves the prototype control flow and measured decision latency for this run. It does not prove Linux kernel scheduling performance or superiority over every fixed scheduler.
